content: The risk of stillbirth or neonatal death increases as pregnancy progresses beyond term, which is approximately 40 weeks of gestation. It remains uncertain whether a policy of inducing labour can effectively reduce these risks. This Cochrane Review, updated from its original publication in 2006 and subsequent updates in 2012 and 2018, aimed to evaluate the effects of labour induction at or beyond 37 weeks of gestation compared to expectant management, where labour is awaited spontaneously or until a later gestational age or a medical indication arises. To conduct this review, researchers searched databases including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform as of July 17, 2019. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving pregnant women at or beyond 37 weeks of gestation, comparing labour induction with expectant management. Trials involving women with prelabour rupture of membranes or those at high risk for complications were excluded. Data were independently assessed for inclusion, risk of bias, and accuracy, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The updated review included 34 RCTs involving over 21,000 women and infants, primarily conducted in high-income settings. These trials compared policies of labour induction, typically after 41 completed weeks of gestation, with expectant management. The trials were generally of low to moderate risk of bias. Labour induction was associated with fewer perinatal deaths from all causes compared to expectant management. Specifically, there were four perinatal deaths in the induction group compared to 25 in the expectant management group, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.31 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.15 to 0.64). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one perinatal death was 544 (95% CI 441 to 1042). Similarly, stillbirths were less frequent in the induction group, with two cases compared to 16 in the expectant management group (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.75). Women in the induction group were less likely to undergo caesarean sections compared to those in the expectant management group (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.95). There was likely little or no difference in the rates of operative vaginal births between the two groups (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.10). Severe perineal trauma was also unlikely to differ significantly between the groups (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.26), though the evidence for this outcome was of low certainty. Postpartum haemorrhage rates were similar between the groups (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.15), as was breastfeeding at discharge (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.04). The length of maternal hospital stay showed very low-certainty evidence, with no clear difference between the groups (mean difference -0.19 days, 95% CI -0.56 to 0.18). Neonatal outcomes were generally better in the induction group, with lower rates of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.96) and fewer infants with Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.96). There was no clear difference in rates of neonatal encephalopathy (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.31) or neonatal trauma (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.49). Neurodevelopmental outcomes in childhood and maternal postnatal depression were not reported in any of the trials. Subgroup analyses revealed no significant differences in outcomes based on the timing of induction (<40 weeks, 40-41 weeks, or ≥41 weeks), parity (primiparous versus multiparous), or cervical status. In conclusion, labour induction at or beyond 37 weeks of gestation reduces the risk of perinatal death compared to expectant management, though the absolute rates of perinatal death are low (0.4 versus 3 deaths per 1000). Induction is also associated with lower caesarean section rates and fewer NICU admissions, without increasing rates of operative vaginal births. Most outcomes were supported by highor moderate-certainty evidence. However, further research is needed to determine the optimal timing for labour induction, assess childhood neurodevelopmental outcomes, and explore the risk profiles and preferences of pregnant women. Tailored counselling may help women make informed decisions about labour induction versus expectant management, particularly for pregnancies extending beyond 41 weeks.
